## Ex: Coffee

::: {.callout title="Question 1"}
A coffee company wants to estimate the average caffeine content in their large brewed coffee. A random sample of 60 cups is tested, and the average caffeine content is found to be 140 mg per cup. Previous studies have shown that the population standard deviation is 12 mg. Construct a 95% confidence interval for the true mean caffeine content.
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
n <- 60
sigma <- 12
alpha <- 0.05
xbar <- 140
z_quant <- qnorm(1-alpha/2)

xbar + c(-1, 1)*z_quant*sigma/sqrt(n)
```

## Ex: Smartphones

::: {.callout title="Question 2"}
A technology company wants to compare the battery life of two smartphone models (Model A and Model B). They conduct 50 tests for Model A and 55 tests for Model B, recording the battery life (in hours). Use the data below to construct a 95% confidence interval for the difference in average battery life for model A and the average battery life for model B (model A minus model B).

```{r, echo = TRUE}
battery_A <- c(12.2, 13.1, 11.7, 10.8, 12.5, 11.3, 13.4, 12.8, 12.1, 13.0, 
               11.9, 12.2, 14.5, 13.1, 12.9, 11.4, 10.9, 14.0, 10.5, 9.8, 
               12.7, 15.2, 10.2, 12.5, 11.8, 14.8, 13.2, 11.7, 9.5, 10.8, 
               13.7, 13.4, 14.3, 14.0, 14.5, 11.3, 10.7, 11.9, 10.1, 13.8)  

battery_B <- c(9.5, 10.2, 9.3, 9.1, 8.7, 9.0, 10.8, 8.5, 8.9, 9.4, 
               11.1, 9.0, 10.5, 9.2, 9.7, 8.8, 10.4, 9.8, 9.9, 9.2, 
               8.7, 9.5, 10.0, 10.2, 11.5, 10.8, 8.9, 9.3, 9.2, 11.0, 
               9.7, 11.2, 10.9, 10.5, 7.9, 7.8, 9.1, 8.3, 10.6, 9.5, 
               8.9, 11.4, 10.8, 10.3, 10.2)  
```
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
max(var(battery_A), var(battery_B)) <= 4*min(var(battery_A), var(battery_B))

t.test(battery_A, battery_B, var.equal = TRUE, conf.level = 0.95)$conf.int
```

## Ex: Insulation

::: {.callout title="Question 3"}
A researcher studies how two different home insulation methods (Method A and Method B) affect energy consumption (in kWh per month). A random sample of 28 households with Method A and 24 households with Method B is taken. Assume the following data are normally distributed and use them to construct a 99% confidence interval for the difference in average energy consumption for the two methods (method B minus method A).

```{r, echo = TRUE}
method_A <- c(320, 310, 305, 315, 300, 310, 290, 310, 305, 295, 315, 320, 
              300, 310, 295, 290, 315, 325, 290, 280, 310, 330, 285, 300, 
              305, 295, 310, 315)  

method_B <- c(400, 420, 390, 385, 410, 450, 375, 400, 380, 395, 390, 420, 
              410, 405, 395, 400, 425, 430, 385, 395, 415, 410, 435, 440)  
```
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
max(var(method_A), var(method_B)) <= 4*min(var(method_A), var(method_B))

t.test(method_B, method_A, var.equal = TRUE, conf.level = 0.99)$conf.int
```

## Ex: Reading

::: {.callout title="Question 4"}
A literacy program wants to estimate the average reading speed (in words per minute) of high school students. A random sample of 40 students had a mean reading speed of 220 words per minute with a standard deviation of 25 words per minute. Construct a 99% confidence interval for the population mean reading speed.
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
xbar <- 220
n <- 40
s <- 25
alpha <- 0.01
t_quant <- qt(1-alpha/2, n-1)

xbar + c(-1, 1)*t_quant*s/sqrt(n)
```

## Ex: Sleep

::: {.callout title="Question 5"}
Researchers study how sleep affects cognitive performance by testing 18 participants on a memory recall task before and after a week of improved sleep habits. The difference in recall scores (after minus before) is recorded, yielding $\bar{x}_d = 3.5, s_d = 5.2$. Assume the data are normally distributed and construct a 90% confidence interval for the mean difference.
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
n <- 18
alpha <- 0.1
xbar_d <- 3.5
s_d <- 5.2
t_quant <- qt(1-alpha/2, n-1)

xbar_d + c(-1, 1)*t_quant*s_d/sqrt(n)
```

## Ex: Keyboards

::: {.callout title="Question 6"}
A study compares reaction times (in milliseconds) for typing on two different types of keyboards (Mechanical and Membrane). A random sample of 35 users for Mechanical keyboards and 30 users for Membrane keyboards is taken. The results are: $\bar{x}_{\text{Mech}} = 120, \bar{x}_{\text{Mem}} = 130, s^2_{\text{Mech}} = 18, s^2_{\text{Mem}} = 22$. Construct a 95% confidence interval for the difference between average reaction times (Mechanical minus Membrane).
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
n_mech <- 35
n_mem <- 30
xbar_mech <- 120
xbar_mem <- 130
s2_mech <- 18
s2_mem <- 22
alpha <- 0.05

max(s2_mech, s2_mem) <= 4*min(s2_mech, s2_mem)
t_quant <- qt(1-alpha/2, n_mech + n_mem - 2)
sp <- sqrt(((n_mech-1)*s2_mech + (n_mem-1)*s2_mem)/(n_mech + n_mem - 2))
se <- sp*sqrt(1/n_mech + 1/n_mem)

(xbar_mech - xbar_mem) + c(-1, 1)*t_quant*se
```

## Ex: Media

::: {.callout title="Question 7"}
A media company wants to estimate the average number of minutes users spend watching online videos daily. A random sample of 40 users is selected, and the following data is recorded. Use the data below to construct a 90% confidence interval for the true average number of minutes users spend watching online videos.

```{r, echo = TRUE}
watch_time <- c(45, 50, 52, 48, 60, 55, 58, 49, 47, 53, 55, 51, 56, 62, 50, 46, 48, 
                52, 54, 57, 64, 66, 58, 50, 47, 45, 52, 55, 58, 54, 60, 62, 50, 48, 47)
```
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
xbar <- mean(watch_time)
s <- sd(watch_time)
n <- length(watch_time)
alpha <- 0.1
t_quant <- qt(1-alpha/2, n-1)

xbar + c(-1, 1)*t_quant*s/sqrt(n)
```

## Ex: Teaching

::: {.callout title="Question 8"}
A study compares two teaching methods (Traditional and Interactive) based on students' final exam scores. Two independent groups of students are randomly assigned: 42 to Traditional and 39 to Interactive. The results show that for Traditional, $\bar{x}_T = 75, s^2_T = 20$, and for Interactive, $\bar{x}_I = 80, s^2_I = 90$. Construct a 99% confidence interval for the difference in the average final exam scores for the two methods (Interactive minus Traditional).
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
xbar_T <- 75
xbar_I <- 80
s2_T <- 20
s2_I <- 90
n_T <- 42
n_I <- 39

max(s2_T, s2_I) <= 4*min(s2_T, s2_I)

df <- ((s2_T/n_T + s2_I/n_I)^2)/(s2_T^2/(n_T^2*(n_T-1)) + s2_I^2/(n_I^2*(n_I-1)))
alpha <- 0.01
t_quant <- qt(1-alpha/2, df)
se <- sqrt(s2_T/n_T + s2_I/n_I)
(xbar_I - xbar_T) + c(-1, 1)*t_quant*se
```

## Ex: Baking

::: {.callout title="Question 9"}
A baker tests a new bread-baking technique by having 35 participants rate the softness of bread before and after using the technique (on a scale from 1 to 10). Use the data below to construct a 95% confidence interval for the mean difference in ratings (new method minus traditional).

```{r, echo = TRUE}
old_ratings <- c(6, 5, 6, 5, 4, 6, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 6, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 4, 4, 5, 6, 5, 3,
                 4, 6, 5, 4, 3, 7, 3, 4, 6, 5, 5, 3)  
new_ratings <- c(8, 8, 8, 8, 7, 7, 7, 7, 7, 7, 7, 7, 8, 7, 8, 7, 7, 6, 6, 7, 5, 4, 7,
                 7, 8, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 5, 5, 4, 8, 7)  
```
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
t.test(new_ratings, old_ratings, paired = TRUE, conf.level = 0.95)$conf.int
```
